title: Roughness and Fresnel — Image Wiki
text:
Roughness and Fresnel
  Two dials that finish a material. Roughness decides how blurry the reflection is; Fresnel makes every surface more reflective at glancing angles. Between them they explain why real objects are never evenly shiny.

  
    Termsurface roughness / Fresnel effect
    Also calledgloss, glossiness, microfacets, grazing-angle reflection, rim sheen
    Not the same asroughness vs bumpiness, roughness vs reflectivity, Fresnel vs rim light
    Read10 min
  

  
    
      On this page
      
        Roughness: how blurry the reflection isFresnel: everything is a mirror at a glancing angleWhy absence of Fresnel is an instant tellCommon mistakes
      
    
  

  Find two pieces of marble in a kitchen showroom, one polished and one honed. Same quarry, same stone, same colour. In the polished slab you can see your face. In the honed slab you can see a soft bright smear where the ceiling light is, and nothing else.
Nothing about how much light those two slabs reflect has changed. Both are stone with the same specular behaviour (Diffuse and specular). What changed is how organised the reflection is. That is roughness, the first of the two dials in this article. The second is the reason a lake is see-through at your feet and a mirror at the far shore: Fresnel.
Roughness: how blurry the reflection is
Zoom in far enough on any surface and it is not flat. A glossy surface is a broken mirror: a field of tiny facets, each obeying the mirror law perfectly, each tilted a little differently (SRC-093). This is the standard model in rendering; PBRT devotes a chapter to it under the name microfacet theory (SRC-090, SRC-091).



Figure by Scratchapixel, What is Shading: Light-Matter interaction, CC BY-NC-ND 4.0. Source.
The yellow rays arrive parallel, as they would from one small lamp. The purple rays are what leaves. Each purple ray is a full-strength mirror bounce — the facet it met obeyed angle-in-equals-angle-out exactly — but because neighbouring facets are tilted differently, no two leave in the same direction. In the lower panel the surface is rougher and the fan is wider still.
Nothing in either panel absorbs anything: the same light leaves, aimed differently. That is the microfacet claim in its rawest form, and it is what the four spheres below say again in brightness curves.



brightness across the surfacesame area = same total lightPolishedmirror, wet glassGlossycar clear-coatSatinbrushed lacquerRoughchalk, unglazed clay

Four panels, one sphere, one lamp in one position. Only the roughness changes.
The curve under each sphere is the brightness of the highlight measured across the surface, and the four curves enclose the same area — the same total light comes back in every case. On the left it is stacked into a narrow spike (a small blown-out hot spot); on the right the same quantity is spread into a low wide hump (a broad dim sheen). Nothing was lost, only redistributed — which is why the right-hand sphere looks less shiny while reflecting just as much.


That trade-off is the same bargain source size drives in Hard and soft light, arriving from the other side. A hard light on a rough surface and a soft light on a polished one can produce highlights of similar size. Only one of them will reflect a recognisable shape, and that is how you tell which is which.



Ximonic (Simo Räsänen), Distorting water reflections at Digermulen port, Hinnøya, Norway, September 2015. Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 4.0.
One surface, one scene, one light — and two roughnesses in the same frame, because a passing boat has roughened half of it. Along the top and behind the boat the water is glass-smooth: the rocks, the grass and the waterline come back as a legible second copy of the shore. In the lower two-thirds the wake has tilted the surface into slow ripples, and the same shore is stretched into unrecognisable bands of green and white — but not into anything dimmer. Only the organisation is gone. Scratchapixel makes this point with a lightly rippled lake: wind does at centimetre scale what microscopic roughness does at micron scale (SRC-093).



Roughness is not bumpiness
Roughness means texture too small to resolve — below the level of a pixel, below the level of your eye at that distance. Its only visible effect is on the sharpness of reflections.
Bumps you can actually see are geometry. Each one has its own lit side and its own tiny shadow, and hard light rakes across them and makes them pop (see Hard and soft light).
Orange peel has both: visible dimples, which are geometry, and a slightly rough finish inside each dimple, which blurs the highlight. Sandblasted glass is the opposite case — visually flat, no bumps at all, and completely diffuse-looking, because all of its structure is below the resolution limit.

Fresnel: everything is a mirror at a glancing angle
The second dial is not a material property you set — it happens to every surface, always. The more edge-on you view a surface, the more of the light it reflects.

100%75%50%25%0%0°30°60°90°straight ongrazingshare of the light reflected at the surface4%39% at 80°100%Reflectivity vs. viewing anglesmooth glass or water, seen from airflat to 50°, then it runs away4%you look straight in→ 100%the rim is edge-on all the way roundthe lampThe same curve on a ballone object, every viewing angle at oncebright rim, duller middle

Left: the real curve, computed for smooth glass seen from air. Almost flat for the first 50° — 4% at 0°, still only 9% at 60° — and then it runs away: 39% by 80°, 100% exactly at the edge. Scratchapixel gives the same two endpoints for a glass ball, ~6% in the middle and effectively total at the rim (SRC-094).
Right: what that curve does to one object. Every angle on it is present at once on a sphere, because the surface turns away from you as you move outward. The middle is where you look straight in — dull. The silhouette is where your line of sight skims the surface — bright, all the way round, including on the side away from the lamp. Only the angle differs.
The small white patch upper left is the ordinary specular highlight, the image of the lamp. The rim brightening is not that, and it is not a lamp behind the ball.


You have seen this all day without naming it. Hold a sheet of paper flat under a lamp and it is matte; tilt it until you are looking almost along it and a sheen appears across the whole page.



Figure by Scratchapixel, Reflection, Refraction and Fresnel, CC BY-NC-ND 4.0. Source.
One flat surface, one photograph, and the whole curve laid out by distance. The red lines are sight lines across the water, all converging on the horizon: at the bottom of the frame you are looking steeply down into it, and by the far shore your line of sight has flattened almost along it. Where it is steep, transmission wins and you read the lake bed pebble by pebble. Where it flattens — the strip just under the horizon — reflection wins, and the water hands back a featureless pale sheet of sky instead. The pebbles are still down there. Nothing hides them but the angle, which is the left-hand curve above walked from 0° at your feet to nearly 90° at the far shore (SRC-094).





Mikhail Kim, Barclays Center Rain Night, 2012. Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 2.0.
The same walk up the frame, on tarmac instead of water, and the road is equally wet from end to end. Near the bottom you can still read the surface itself: asphalt grain, yellow lane lines, the white "ONLY" lettering. Further away the road stops being a road and becomes a mirror — signage, street lamps and lit facade all stretched into long streaks running toward you.
The streaks are long for a second reason: this is Fresnel and roughness at once, each source smeared along the direction the ripples tilt, as in the harbour photograph above. A still film of water would give short sharp inverted copies instead.


Why absence of Fresnel is an instant tell
Because Fresnel applies to every surface without exception, a real curved object almost never has the same shininess across its whole surface. A ball lit from one side has a highlight where the light is, and a general brightening around its whole silhouette that has nothing to do with where the light is.
Take that rim brightening away and a ball becomes a flat coloured disc with a sticker on it, skin turns to rubber, glass turns to tinted plastic and water turns to coloured jelly. The opposite failure is even gloss everywhere, rim identical to centre. Nothing physical does that either.



You change
What happens




Polish the surface
reflection sharpens, highlight shrinks and brightens


Roughen the surface
reflection blurs, highlight spreads and dims


Wet the surface
roughness drops sharply — water fills the micro-texture, so wet things go glossy and darker


Move to a glancing view
reflectivity rises toward 100% at every point you see edge-on


Curve the surface
the rim is automatically at a glancing angle, so it brightens


Make it metal
reflectivity is already high face-on, so the rim effect is subtle — see Metal and everything else



Metals follow a different Fresnel formula from dielectrics (SRC-094), which is why the rise toward their rim is much less dramatic: they start out reflecting a lot at every angle.
Common mistakes

"Rough means less reflective." No. It means the same reflection, spread out. Polished and honed marble reflect the same amount of light. Only the organisation differs.
"Fresnel is a rim light." A rim light is a lamp behind the subject making an actual bright edge. Fresnel is a change in reflectivity, and what it shows you is whatever happens to be in the mirror direction — which might be a bright sky or a dark wall. If the environment behind the object is dark, Fresnel makes the rim darker, not brighter.
"Glossy things are brighter." Gloss concentrates the same light into a smaller area, so it reads brighter in that spot and darker everywhere else. Side by side, a glossy black car has more black in it than a matte black one, not less.
"Roughness and bumpiness are the same slider." A surface can be microscopically polished and visibly lumpy (a hammered copper bowl), or microscopically rough and geometrically perfect (frosted acrylic).
"Wet just means darker." Wetting does two things at once: it fills the micro-roughness, sharpening reflections, and it lets more light into the material before it comes back, deepening the diffuse colour. Wet sand is darker and glossier, and both need to be present.


Checking gloss and Fresnel in five seconds

Find a highlight. Can you make out the shape of the source inside it, or is it a smear? Sharp shape means a smooth surface.
Look at the rim of any curved object. Is it brighter, or darker, than the middle in a way that does not track the light direction? Some difference should be there.
Compare two surfaces you would expect to differ — glass vs. cloth, wet vs. dry pavement. Do their reflections differ in sharpness, not just brightness?
Check the roughness is consistent with the visible texture. Rough-looking woven fabric with a mirror highlight, or smooth chrome with a broad matte sheen, is a contradiction.
If everything in the frame is evenly shiny at every angle, the picture was not made by physics.



  
    
      Read next
      
        
          
            
              Diffuse and specular
              Light hitting a surface either goes in and comes back out coloured, or bounces straight off keeping the light's own colour. Almost everything a material looks like follows from the split between those two.
            
          
        
          
            
              Metal and everything else
              Metals have almost no colour of their own and show you the room instead; everything else gets its colour from underneath and reflects the light's own colour on top. This is the sharpest material test you can run on an image.
            
          
        
          
            
              Hard and soft light
              Whether shadows have crisp edges or fade gradually. It is decided by one thing — how big the light looks from where the subject is standing.
